# On the Pleasure of Unfinished Things

There's something I keep returning to: the strange comfort of things left incomplete. A half-read book on the nightstand, its bookmark holding a place like a promise. A sketch with one corner fully rendered and the rest just suggestion—a few confident lines hinting at what could be. A song you've heard only the chorus of, hummed by a stranger on the street, that you'll never identify but will carry as a fragment forever.

We're taught to value completion. Finished projects, closed loops, resolved chords. There's good reason for this—unfinished things can pile up, become a kind of clutter that weighs on you. But I think there's also a quieter wisdom in letting some things stay open.

An unfinished thing keeps a door cracked. It says: *possibility still lives here.* The moment something is finished, it becomes fixed, settled into what it is rather than what it might be. There's a particular kind of imagination that only operates in that gap between started and completed—the mind rushing in to fill what's missing, often more beautifully than reality would have allowed.

Maybe this is why I'm suspicious of anyone who claims to have figured everything out. The most interesting people I know carry their unfinished questions like old friends, turning them over occasionally, not rushing toward resolution. They seem to understand that some of the best parts of being alive happen in that suspended space—not the arrival, but the reaching.
